subject: Computer Networking
title: Mainframes and Terminals
description: A micro-lesson that makes Mainframes and Terminals usable.

hook.text: In the 1960s, one giant computer served an entire building. Users shared it through dumb terminals on their desks.

buildup.text: Terminals had no processing power. They sent keystrokes to the mainframe and displayed whatever it sent back.

discovery.text: Time-sharing let dozens of users work on one mainframe simultaneously. Each got a slice of CPU time.

twist.text: Terminals connected via dedicated serial cables. Each new user meant another physical wire — expensive and rigid.

climax.text: This centralized model planted the seed: if terminals could connect over phone lines, distance wouldn't matter.

punchline.text: Mainframes proved sharing was possible. Networks removed the distance barrier.

quiz.question: What did time-sharing allow on mainframes?
options: Multiple users to share one computer simultaneously

details.summary: Before networking, computing was centralized on mainframes accessed through dumb terminals. Users shared a single powerful computer via time-sharing.
details.whyItMatters: The mainframe-terminal model is the ancestor of cloud computing. History cycles between centralized and distributed computing, and understanding the pattern reveals where technology is heading.
takeaways: Mainframes were shared by many users through terminals
Time-sharing gave each user the illusion of dedicated access
The thin-client model returned with web apps and cloud computing

faq.question: What was time-sharing on a mainframe?
faq.answer: The mainframe rapidly switched between users, giving each a small slice of processing time. Each user appeared to have the computer to themselves. This was the first form of multi-user computing and inspired later concepts of virtual machines and cloud instances.

faq.question: How is cloud computing similar to the mainframe era?
faq.answer: Cloud computing centralizes processing in data centers accessed through thin clients like browsers. Users share hardware through virtualization, just as mainframe users shared through time-sharing. The cycle from centralized to distributed and back continues to repeat.
